Stories / Martinique · Dominica · Versailles · 1778–1779

Story · American War of Independence, 18th century

Martinique, 1778–1779: Bouillé and Grasse, a war plan in cipher

September 1778: France has been at war with Britain since the summer. The marquis de Bouillé, governor general of the Windward Islands, has just taken Dominica. He writes in cipher to the Navy minister that he lacks the men to go further. A year later, with the comte de Grasse, he sends him a whole war plan, also in cipher. The French overseas archives list these pieces as “not deciphered”.

A story by Brice Dudout · reading with Claude · documents: Archives nationales d’outre-mer (Aix-en-Provence), COL C8 A 77 ff. 88 and 101, C8 A 76 f. 196 · published 14 November 2026

“This squadron and these troops, though not large, will nevertheless be able to do great things, being easier to move, and falling upon the enemy unawares.”

Plan by Grasse and Bouillé, Martinique, 4 August 1779 (ciphered passage, read with the table of Bouillé’s cipher; our translation).

What is new, what was known

Known. Bouillé’s capture of Dominica (7 September 1778), the loss of St Lucia in December, and Grasse’s great campaign of 1781 are well known.[3][4] The online inventory of the Archives nationales d’outre-mer lists the two 1778 letters as “not deciphered” and takes the 1779 memorandum for “another cipher prepared by MM. de Bouillé and de Grasse”.[1]

What we add, as far as we know. (1) The first published decipherment of Bouillé’s two letters of 1778: read, 448 of 458 words certain or probable (97.8%). (2) The first published decipherment of the war plan of Grasse and Bouillé of 4 August 1779: read, 768 of 794 words certain or probable (96.7%); with its four ciphered tables, 1,206 of 1,266 (95.3%). (3) A plan that foreshadows, two years ahead, the way Grasse would wage war in 1781.

Dominica and the 817 men

Bouillé reached Martinique in 1777. As soon as news of the war arrived in the islands, he attacked Dominica, a British island lying between Martinique and Guadeloupe, and took it on 7 September 1778.[3] Ten days later he wrote in cipher to Sartine:

“I await all the more impatiently the recruits that the minister of war has announced to me, as the gap of eight hundred and seventeen men does not yet allow me to undertake anything against some English islands, since I could not put a garrison there without stripping Martinique, where there remain […] only three thousand three hundred effective men.”

On 5 December he sent, also in cipher, the return of Dominica’s new garrison: 1,072 men, half from Martinique and half from Guadeloupe, including 81 “Volontaires de Bouillé” and 222 “gens de couleur” (free men of colour). A second table gives the troops of Martinique: 1,031 men short of establishment. A few days later the British took St Lucia, and d’Estaing’s squadron failed to retake it.[5] Bouillé’s numbers explain why he could not run from one island to the next.

The plan of 1779

The comte de Grasse, chef d’escadre, reached the islands early in 1779 with reinforcements for d’Estaing.[4] With Bouillé he drew up a project “on the surest means of protecting the French colonies in America and of attacking those of the English”. A first copy, dated 31 March, is in another cipher (the “cipher of 1777”); the second, of 4 August, is in Bouillé’s.[1] The idea fits in a few lines: the Windward Islands fear the British only in winter; so what is needed is a light squadron — eight ships of the line, four frigates, two corvettes, three storeships and 2,500 to 2,600 men — leaving Europe at the end of October and based at Martinique.

“This squadron and these troops, after protecting all our colonies during their stay in the Windward Islands, will be able to act against those of the English […], going in turn to the English Windward and Leeward Islands, to New England, to the region of Florida, to St Augustine, to Pensacola, to the Banks of Newfoundland, where one may seize that island and destroy the cod fishery in all that region […].”

Secrecy, surprise, mobility: “always in motion, it will hardly be liable to interception”. Bouillé offers to command the land forces, “above all if M. le comte de Grasse is charged with directing those at sea”. The memorandum ends with the ambition to “restore to our arms the lustre they have recently lost in America”, probably an allusion to St Lucia. Four ciphered tables give the artillery, the park (1,045,994 livres in weight), the troops and the squadron (9,220 men); their totals check. At the foot of the last, Bouillé notes in clear that Grasse, being absent, could not sign.

Two years later

The plan was not carried out as written. But in March 1781 Grasse left Brest with some twenty ships of the line. With Bouillé he took Tobago in June; then, during the hurricane season, he sailed north, embarked troops at Saint-Domingue, received Spanish money from Havana, and closed Chesapeake Bay: Yorktown. In November he was back in the Windward Islands; Bouillé took St Eustatius from the British, then St Kitts in February 1782.[4][3] The Spanish, for their part, took Pensacola in May 1781.[6]

The pattern of 1779 — defend the islands in winter, strike far away the rest of the year, act with Spain, return in November — is that of the 1781 campaign. This is a comparison, not a proven line of descent: we have found no document linking the 1779 plan to the orders of 1781.

Bouillé’s cipher

  • A code of about 850 numbers for letters, syllables and words, with homophones (361 = de, 250 = l’, 607 = le, 817 = s) and code names (267 = Martinique, 428 = Guadeloupe, 138 = Dominica).
  • Distinct from the minister’s table and from the “cipher of 1777” of the March copy.
  • No period key found: the table was rebuilt from letters of 1779–1782 in the same series that carry their decipherment in pencil between the lines or a copy in clear.

How we read it

  1. Transcription of the numbers from the images of the Archives nationales d’outre-mer, frozen by SHA-256 hash before reading.
  2. A table learned from period cipher + clear pairs (five glossed letters of 1779, then three pairs of 1780–1782), frozen by hash.
  3. Held-out validations, under a protocol written in advance, each on a fresh piece, against 200 control tables: for the 1778 letters, C8 A 77 f. 123 (words 0.865, characters 0.850; best control 0.038 / 0.165), then f. 70 (0.894 / 0.897; 0.182 / 0.174); for the 1779 plan, Bouillé’s memorandum of 14 September 1781 (C8 A 80 ff. 113–115, 485 numbers: 0.825 / 0.889; 0.149 / 0.089).
  4. The reading, under Daniel Bourdeau’s rule (95% of words read by sense): 1778 letters, 437 certain and 11 probable of 458 (97.8%); 1779 plan, 759 certain and 9 probable of 794 (96.7%).

What remains uncertain

  • Restored words. 7 words in the 1778 letters and 22 in the 1779 text are restored from sense; they are marked in the entries. One value in the tables is probably misread (a 2,000-livre gap on a carried total).
  • The March 1779 copy (C8 A 76 f. 191, “cipher of 1777”) reads at 98.0%, but its table was validated only on a portion already used twice: we present it only as a complement, in the entry.
  • Grasse’s letter of April 1779, in that same cipher, is read only in part (89.7%).
  • Prior work. Checked on 28 October and again on 14 November 2026: inventory and records of the Archives nationales d’outre-mer, Daniel Bourdeau’s repository (targets bouille1778 and grassebouille1779, our readings), web search. Catalogues checked on 14 November (Archives nationales, Marine B4; BnF, Archives et manuscrits; ANOM inventory): no clear copy recorded. Marine B4 195 f. 3 holds the keys of Bouillé’s ciphers (1778–1782) and B4 161 f. 374 “Lettres de Bouillé à Sartine (chiffre)”, not consulted. The British intercepted this mail: The National Archives (Kew) holds duplicates of letters from Bouillé to Sartine of July–August 1779 and February 1780 described as “deciphered” (CO 166/1/31–36, Daniel Bourdeau’s catalogue no. 867), not digitised; according to the catalogue, our documents are not among them.
  • No image of the documents: the online images of the Archives nationales d’outre-mer carry no reuse licence; they are not reproduced. The illustration is a schematic of places, not an accurate map.
